title: FAST Scholarships and Financial Aid: What to Know Before You Apply
excerpt: FAST offers both merit-based and need-based financial support — here's how each actually works, who qualifies, and what to check before assuming a scholarship will cover your costs.

content.text: Two different kinds of support, not one

FAST-NUCES runs two distinct categories of financial assistance: merit-based scholarships for top academic performers, and need-based support for students who can demonstrate genuine financial hardship. These aren't interchangeable, and understanding which one you might actually qualify for — possibly both, at different points in your degree — matters more than treating "scholarship" as one vague category.

Scholarship criteria, amounts, and availability are set by FAST and can change between semesters and campuses. This post reflects FAST's own published financial aid framework, but exact current terms should always be confirmed directly at nu.edu.pk or with your specific campus's student affairs office before you factor any aid into your admission decision.
Merit-based scholarships: what they actually cover

FAST's merit scholarship is awarded to the top three position holders of each examination board, and separately, to the top three position holders in the NU admission merit list at each campus. Where awarded, it covers 100% of tuition fees for all eight regular semesters of a bachelor's degree — a genuinely significant award if you qualify, not a partial waiver.

The catch is that this isn't a one-time award you can coast on. Students who receive it must maintain a CGPA of 3.00 or higher every semester to keep it — dropping below that threshold means losing the scholarship going forward, not just that semester's installment.

items: Awarded to top 3 position holders per examination board
Also awarded to top 3 position holders in each campus's admission merit list
Requires maintaining a semester CGPA of 3.00+ to continue

content.text: Need-based support: loans, not automatic waivers

For students facing genuine financial hardship, FAST's primary need-based mechanism is an interest-free study loan — not an outright grant — aimed at what the university describes as "bright indigent students." This assistance is limited specifically to tuition fees, is subject to renewal each semester based on your academic performance, and is discontinued if your CGPA falls below the university's specified minimum.

It's worth being clear-eyed about what this means practically: an interest-free loan reduces the immediate financial burden significantly, since you're not paying interest on top of tuition, but it isn't free money in the way a full scholarship is — you (or your family) are still expected to repay it over time.

"Bright indigent students" and the specific financial thresholds used to determine eligibility aren't fixed public numbers — the assessment process and required documentation should be confirmed directly with FAST's financial aid office, since this is exactly the kind of detail that varies by individual case and campus.

Beyond FAST's own merit and need-based schemes, several other funding sources are associated with the university, including a recognized interest-free education loan program (Qarz-e-Hasna, administered through the Ihsan Trust) available on a need-cum-merit basis across FAST's campuses, provincial government scholarships (a Punjab government scheme has been associated with a defined number of scholarships for Punjab-domicile students, generally covering roughly half of tuition with the remainder available as an interest-free loan; a Sindh government scheme operates on a need-cum-merit basis for the Karachi campus), and several community and foundation-based scholarships, including ones associated with the Memon Community, the Bohra Community, and the Aga Khan Foundation.

items: Qarz-e-Hasna (Ihsan Trust): interest-free education loan, need-cum-merit basis, available across campuses
Provincial government schemes: availability and terms differ by province and campus — Punjab and Sindh-linked schemes have both been referenced in FAST's own materials
Community/foundation scholarships: several community-specific and foundation-backed options exist alongside the university's own schemes

content.text: The exact number of provincial scholarships available, their coverage percentage, and eligibility (such as domicile requirements) change based on government allocation each year — treat any specific figure here as illustrative of the kind of support that exists, not a guaranteed current number, and confirm directly with the relevant provincial scheme and FAST's financial aid office.
What this means for your application strategy

If a merit scholarship is realistically within reach for you — meaning you're competitive for a top-3 board position or a top-3 campus merit rank — it's worth treating that as a genuine goal worth the extra push in your final exam or entry test preparation, not just a long-shot bonus. The gap between "close to top 3" and "actually top 3" can be the difference between paying full tuition and paying none of it.

If you're instead looking at need-based support, the more useful step than guessing at eligibility is contacting FAST's financial aid office directly, ideally before or immediately after you're admitted, since loan-based aid tends to involve a documented application process rather than an automatic determination based on your admission application alone.

Either way, don't let uncertainty about cost stop you from applying in the first place — FAST's own published framework makes clear that meaningful support exists for both high performers and students facing genuine financial hardship, but the specifics of which category you'd fall into, and exactly what that means in rupees, are worth confirming directly rather than assuming from general descriptions like this one.

items.answer: The top three position holders of each examination board, and separately, the top three position holders in the NU admission merit list at each campus.

items.answer: It's an interest-free study loan limited to tuition fees, not an outright grant — it's still expected to be repaid over time, and is subject to renewal each semester based on academic performance.

items.question: Are there financial aid options beyond FAST's own scholarships and loans?
items.answer: Yes — including the Qarz-e-Hasna interest-free loan program through the Ihsan Trust, provincial government schemes that vary by province and campus, and several community and foundation-based scholarships.
